snippet.title: What is "The Thinker" actually thinking about? - Noah Charney
snippet.description:
Get to know Auguste Rodin’s infamous sculpture “The Thinker,” and find out who was the inspiration for this masterpiece.

--

Contrary to popular belief, "The Thinker" sculpture isn’t just a universal symbol of eternal contemplation. French sculptor Auguste Rodin intended it to represent a specific person— and fit into a much larger piece featuring the fiery pits of Hell. So, who was "The Thinker," and what was he actually thinking? Noah Charney digs into the secrets of this infamous work of art.

Lesson by Noah Charney, directed by Avi Ofer.

snippet.title: Suzannah Lipscomb Uncovers The Final Days Of Henry VIII & Anne Boleyn
snippet.description:
The romance between Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn is frequently remembered as a legendary tale of royal passion, but the reality hidden within the palace walls was far darker and more violent than any fiction. Henry was a charismatic, athletic monarch tormented by his inability to secure a male heir, a desperate pursuit that eventually drove him to alienate his allies, divide his kingdom, and sever ties with Rome. Anne was a brilliant, sophisticated woman who brought a dangerous flash of modern European glamour to a strict English court, unknowingly placing herself directly in the crosshairs of a ruthless political machine. When devastating personal tragedies and a near-fatal accident began to unravel the king's stability, the grand promises of their early love quickly mutated into paranoia and betrayal. This investigation strips away the centuries of romantic myth to expose how a single relationship altered the faith of a nation and why the final, shocking collapse of their marriage became the most dangerous scandal of the age.

snippet.description:
Dig into the history of medieval European castles, and explore how the design of these formidable fortresses evolved over time.

Medieval European castles weren’t just for passive defense and withstanding enemy onslaughts; they were symbols of power, private residences, and hubs of governance. Castles regularly served as bases for launching attacks and as a way to control local populations. So, how were these formidable fortresses built? Connor C. Wilson explores how the design of these structures evolved over time.

snippet.title: Trapped In The Pacific: The Prohibited Rescue That Cost A Pilot’s Life
snippet.description:
World War II was fought by the very hands of small-town America, where teenagers lied about their age to wear a uniform and everyday citizens planted victory gardens. But for the crew of the B-29 bomber Dragon Lady, the harsh reality of war struck in the skies over Yokohama. Ripped apart by enemy flack and consumed by an uncontrollable electrical fire, the crew was forced into a blind, terrifying crash landing into the deep Pacific. Stranded in enemy waters with zero communication and critically injured men, their chances of survival dwindled by the minute.

Miles away on the volcanic ash of Iwo Jima, a twenty-two-year-old PBY Catalina pilot named Royal A. Stratton answered the call. Defying direct military protocol, Stratton risked everything to land his flying boat directly into treacherous ten-foot ocean swells. What followed was the most successful lifeguard submarine rescue mission in naval history, but it came at an unthinkable price. This emotional documentary features rare, firsthand accounts from the veterans who lived through the chaos, detailing a breathtaking story of survival, a horrific cockpit accident, and the enduring legacy of a hero who gave everything so his brothers could make it home.

Tristan Hughes and Matt Lewis (host of 'Gone Medieval') have a lively debate about the blurred boundary between the ancient and medieval worlds. Can Tristan champion Roman Emperor Justinian as an Ancient?  What about Charlemagne?  Which period can lay claim to the worst year in history? snippet.title: What Medieval Outlaws Actually Ate While Hiding in the Forest
snippet.description:
Life as an outlaw in the Middle Ages wasn’t romantic it was harsh, uncertain, and heavily dependent on whatever food could be found, traded, or stolen while avoiding capture.

In this video, we explore what medieval fugitives and forest outlaws likely ate to survive while living away from towns and farmland.

What You’ll Discover:
How outlaws relied on foraging, hunting, and simple camp cooking
Wild foods commonly found in medieval forests
The role of dried foods, bread, and preserved meat
Why fire, smoke, and movement had to be carefully managed
The reality of survival outside normal society

There were no stocked supplies or guaranteed meals survival depended on knowledge of the land and constant adaptation.

No comfort. No security. Just whatever could keep you alive one more day.

snippet.title: The REAL reasons European colonialism was possible
snippet.description:
Contrary to popular belief, the European colonization of the Americas was made possible not by the Europeans having superior technology, but by the inadvertent introduction of pathogens from the Eastern Hemisphere that had not previously been present in the Americas.

This accounts for the fact that when the Europeans were colonizing the Americas in the 1500s and 1600s, they were not also colonizing Africa and Asia (with a few exceptions). It was not possible for the Europeans to colonize most parts of Africa and Asia at the time, because the people there already had the same technologies and the same diseases that the Europeans had.

Of course, Europeans did end up colonizing Africa and Asia, but not until the 1800s. This was suddenly possible then, when it hadn't been earlier, because the Industrial Revolution happened to begin in Europe then. Within just a few generations, industrial technology also spread to the rest of the world, but by then the Europeans and people of European descent had managed to establish their preeminence in world affairs.

The economic, military, and technological superiority of the countries of Europe and of people of European descent traces back only as far as the Industrial Revolution in the 1800s. Before that, Europeans had no advantages over the countries of Asia and Africa.

snippet.title: 1666: The Firestorm That Destroyed 85% of Medieval London (England)
snippet.description:
In this documentary-style deep dive, we are stepping into the ashes to explore the immediate, untold aftermath of one of history's most monumental infernos. When the smoke finally cleared, 85% of the medieval metropolis was simply gone. With no clean water, no food storehouses, and winter rapidly approaching, the displaced citizens were forced into sprawling, muddy refugee camps. We explore the grueling daily reality of these survivors, the historical unrest that gripped the ruined streets, and the extreme, unprecedented measures taken to prevent total societal collapse.

From the shattered cobblestones to the visionary blueprints of a new era, discover how a resilient population managed to endure the unimaginable and lay the indestructible brick foundations for a modern metropolis. If you enjoy uncovering the incredible human spirit and the forgotten realities of the past, make sure to like the video and subscribe for more historical journeys!

What this video covers:

The Scale of Destruction: A look at the staggering loss of 13,200 homes and the complete erasure of medieval London's street map.

The Survival Crisis: How 100,000 newly homeless citizens battled exposure, starvation, and a lack of clean water in makeshift tent cities.

Total Infrastructure Collapse: The devastating impact of losing granaries, water pipes, and the economic epicenter of the Royal Exchange.

The Rebuilding Effort: How strict new laws, stone mandates, and sheer physical labor transformed a smoking crater into a modern superpower.

snippet.title: How Did Medieval Knights Know Who (Not) To Kill?
snippet.description:
Medieval battles weren’t as chaotic as movies make them seem. While combat could be brutal, there were rules, signals, and social codes that helped knights distinguish friend from foe and sometimes decide who to spare.

In this video, we explore how identification, loyalty, and battlefield customs shaped who knights targeted (and who they didn’t).

You’ll Discover:
How heraldry (coats of arms) identified knights in battle
The role of banners, colors, and symbols on the battlefield
Why armor and surcoats displayed family or faction identity
The practice of capturing nobles for ransom instead of killing
How religion and chivalric codes influenced behavior

It wasn’t perfect confusion still happened but there were systems in place to reduce it.

Sometimes survival wasn’t just about fighting… it was about knowing who you were fighting.

snippet.title: The Mary Rose: The Deadly Design Flaw Hidden Inside History's Most Famous Ship
snippet.description:
From ancient Egyptian sailboats to modern megaships, journey through the awe-inspiring evolution of ship engineering and discover how ancient innovations shaped our world.

In this captivating deep dive into maritime engineering, we unveil how early civilizations pushed technological boundaries, constructing wonders like the Khufu Ship with primitive tools and ingenuity. Explore how inventions such as multi-hull canoes in Polynesia, the revolutionary sails of Egypt, and the robust clinker-built Viking longships forever expanded humanity’s reach. Learn how pivotal breakthroughs—like the addition of gunports to warships and the development of multi-masted vessels—fueled global exploration, massive trade networks, naval dominance, and even the spread of empires.

We trace the journey from wooden ships that braved oceans to today’s colossal steel giants, revealing the engineering challenges and environmental impacts of shipbuilding. Hear about legendary finds like Sutton Hoo and the raising of the Tudor warship Mary Rose, uncovering untold stories of craftsmanship and innovation. Whether you’re fascinated by the physics of buoyancy, the secrets of ancient carpentry, or the high-tech stealth of today’s battleships, this video offers a thrilling look at ships’ vital role in trade, warfare, discovery, and the interconnected global economy.

snippet.title: The Irish Migrations: That Changed Britain Forever (400–600 AD)
snippet.description:
What really happened after Rome left Britain?This video explores the hidden story of the Irish migrations that reshaped western Britain during the early medieval period (400–700 AD). Instead of a silent collapse, Britain became a place of movement, cultural exchange, and everyday survival.

We dive into how people actually lived during this time—how homes were built, what daily life looked like, how communities formed, and how Irish and Britons interacted with each other. From rural farmsteads and smoky houses to muddy paths and shared traditions, this is a grounded, human look at a period often misunderstood.

What this video covers:
The Irish migrations into Wales and western Britain
How people reacted—conflict, coexistence, and integration
Daily life: farming, food, and routines
Houses and settlements (ringforts, rural homes)
Hygiene and living conditions
How relationships and marriages formed between communities

Sources:
https://www.thecollector.com/dark-ages-irish-migrations/
https://www.britannica.com/biography/Cunedda-Wledig
https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/medieval-ireland/
https://www.intarch.ac.uk/journal/issue42/6/
https://www.britishmuseum.org/
https://www.global.oup.com/academic/product/life-in-early-medieval-wales-9780198733218
